body:
What Is a Lens?

A spherical lens is a transparent optical element bounded by 2 surfaces, at least 1 of which is spherical. It changes the direction of transmitted light through refraction.

Unlike a mirror, which forms images by reflection, a lens forms images mainly by the refraction of light passing through its surfaces.

Convex Lens

A typical double-convex lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges. When surrounded by air and made of ordinary glass or similar material, it converges rays that arrive parallel to its principal axis.

It is therefore called a converging lens.

The point at which parallel rays meet after passing through the convex lens is its principal focus on the opposite side of the lens.

Concave Lens

A typical double-concave lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges. In air, it causes parallel incident rays to diverge after refraction.

It is therefore called a diverging lens.

The refracted rays appear to originate from a principal focus on the same side of the lens as the incoming light.

Important Parts of a Spherical Lens

  • Principal axis: The straight line passing through the centres of curvature of the lens surfaces.
  • Optical centre (O): The central point through which a ray is treated as passing undeviated in the thin-lens approximation.
  • Principal focus: The point at which rays parallel to the principal axis meet after refraction, or from which they appear to diverge.
  • Focal length (f): The distance between the optical centre and a principal focus.
  • Aperture: The effective diameter of the lens through which light passes.

A lens has 2 principal foci, one associated with light entering from each side. They are commonly labelled F1 and F2.

In standard ray diagrams, light approaches from the left. F1 is on the object side, while F2 is on the opposite side.

Principal Rays Used to Draw Lens Images

For a thin lens, 2 appropriately chosen rays from a point of the object are sufficient to determine the corresponding image point.

  1. Ray parallel to the principal axis: After passing through a convex lens, it goes through F2. After a concave lens, it diverges as though it came from F1.
  2. Ray through F1 (convex lens) or directed toward F2 (concave lens): It emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction.
  3. Ray through the optical centre O: In the thin-lens approximation, it passes without a change in direction.

For a real image, actual refracted rays meet. For a virtual image, the refracted rays diverge and their backward extensions meet.

Lens Focal Length and Mirror Radius

For a spherical mirror of small aperture, focal length is related to the radius of curvature by R = 2f. This relationship should not be applied indiscriminately to lenses.

A lens is bounded by 2 surfaces, and its focal length depends on its curvature and refractive properties. At this level, its focal length is treated as a given quantity.

A convex lens is converging and ordinarily has positive focal length under the New Cartesian Sign Convention. A concave lens is diverging and has negative focal length.

Prelims focus

  • Convex lens: thicker at the centre and converging in air.
  • Concave lens: thinner at the centre and diverging in air.
  • A lens has 2 principal foci.
  • A ray through the optical centre travels undeviated in the thin-lens approximation.
  • Convex lens focal length is positive; concave lens focal length is negative.
  • Trap: The spherical-mirror relationship R = 2f is not a general formula for lenses.

[NCERT, Science, Class VII, Chapter 15, 'Light', Section 15.5, printed pp. 183–185; NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.3.3 and 9.3.5, Figures 9.12–9.15, printed pp. 150–154.]

title: Convex and Concave Lenses: Structure, Focus and Principal Rays

body:
How a Convex Lens Produces Different Images

A convex lens converges parallel rays of light. However, the image formed by a convex lens is not always real or inverted. Its nature depends on the object's distance from the optical centre compared with the focal length.

In standard lens diagrams, O is the optical centre, F1 is the principal focus on the object side and F2 is the principal focus on the opposite side. The points 2F1 and 2F2 are at twice the focal length from O.

6 Standard Positions of the Object

Object positionImage positionRelative sizeNature
At infinityAt F2Highly diminishedReal, inverted
Beyond 2F1Between F2 and 2F2DiminishedReal, inverted
At 2F1At 2F2Same sizeReal, inverted
Between F1 and 2F1Beyond 2F2EnlargedReal, inverted
At F1At infinityHighly enlargedReal, inverted in the ideal ray model
Between F1 and OOn the same side as the objectEnlargedVirtual, erect

Real Images Produced by a Convex Lens

Object Beyond Twice the Focal Length

When the object is placed beyond 2F1, a ray parallel to the principal axis is refracted through F2. A second ray through the optical centre travels without deviation in the thin-lens approximation.

The 2 rays meet between F2 and 2F2, producing a real, inverted and diminished image.

Object at Twice the Focal Length

When an object is placed at 2F1, its image is formed at 2F2. The image is real, inverted and equal in size to the object.

Object Between F1 and 2F1

When the object lies between the principal focus and twice the focal length, its real image forms beyond 2F2. It is inverted and enlarged.

Object at F1

When an object is at the principal focus, rays emerging from the lens from a given object point become parallel in the ideal ray model. The image is described as forming at infinity.

A screen placed at a finite distance cannot capture a sharp image in this ideal arrangement.

Virtual Image Produced by a Convex Lens

When the object is between F1 and O, the emerging rays diverge. Their backward extensions meet on the same side of the lens as the object.

The image is virtual, erect and enlarged. It cannot be projected onto a screen.

Applications of Convex Lenses

  • Magnifying glass: An object placed inside the focal length produces a virtual, erect and enlarged image.
  • Camera: A convex lens system forms a real image on the image sensor.
  • Projection: A suitably positioned convex lens forms a real enlarged image on a screen.

These applications differ mainly in where the object and the receiving surface are positioned relative to the lens and its focal points.

For a real object beyond the focal length, a convex lens produces a real, inverted image. For an object inside the focal length, it produces a virtual, erect and enlarged image.

Prelims focus

  • Beyond 2F1: diminished image between F2 and 2F2.
  • At 2F1: equal-sized image at 2F2.
  • Between F1 and 2F1: enlarged real image beyond 2F2.
  • At F1: image at infinity in the ideal ray model.
  • Inside F1: virtual, erect and enlarged image.
  • Trap: A convex lens does not always produce a real image.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.3.4–9.3.5, Table 9.4 and Figure 9.16, printed pp. 152–155.]

pictures.alt: An object beyond 2F1 sends rays through a convex lens that meet between F2 and 2F2, forming a smaller, inverted real image.
pictures.caption: A convex lens forms a real, inverted and diminished image when the object lies beyond 2F.

pictures.alt: An object between F1 and O forms an enlarged upright virtual image where dashed backward extensions of diverging refracted rays meet.
pictures.caption: A convex lens acts as a magnifying glass when the object lies within its focal length.

title: Image Formation by a Convex Lens

body:
How a Concave Lens Forms Images

A concave lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges and acts as a diverging lens when surrounded by air.

When parallel rays enter a concave lens, they spread apart after refraction. Their backward extensions appear to meet at the principal focus on the same side of the lens as the incident light.

For a real object placed in front of an ordinary concave lens, the refracted rays diverge and do not actually meet. Their backward extensions determine the virtual image position.

A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of a real object placed in front of it.

Standard Image Positions

Object positionImage positionSizeNature
At infinityAt F1 on the object sideHighly diminishedVirtual, erect
At any finite distance in frontBetween F1 and O on the object sideDiminishedVirtual, erect

Ray Diagram of a Concave Lens

To construct the image, consider 2 rays from the upper end of the object.

  1. A ray parallel to the principal axis diverges after passing through the lens. Its backward extension passes through F1.
  2. A ray passing through the optical centre O continues without deviation in the thin-lens approximation.

The backward extensions meet between F1 and O. This gives the position of the virtual image.

Moving the object farther away causes the image to become smaller and approach F1. Moving it closer makes the image larger, but it remains diminished for a real object at a finite distance.

Concave Lens and Convex Lens Compared

PropertyConvex lensConcave lens
Typical shapeThicker at centreThinner at centre
Effect on parallel raysConvergesDiverges
Focal length signPositiveNegative
Image of real objectReal or virtualAlways virtual
Image orientationInverted or erectAlways erect

Applications in Vision Correction

A concave lens is used to correct myopia or near-sightedness. In myopia, distant objects are not seen clearly because their images would form in front of the retina. A suitable diverging lens helps shift the focus onto the retina.

A convex lens is used to correct hypermetropia or far-sightedness, where light from nearby objects would otherwise focus behind the retina. A suitable converging lens helps bring the image onto the retina.

The important optical distinction is that a concave lens reduces the convergence of incoming light, while a convex lens increases it.

Prelims focus

  • A concave lens is diverging.
  • Its focal length is negative.
  • For a real object, it always produces a virtual, erect and diminished image.
  • The finite-object image lies between F1 and O.
  • A concave lens is used to correct myopia.
  • Trap: The image formed by a concave lens cannot be captured on a screen.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.3.4–9.3.5, Table 9.5 and Figure 9.17, printed pp. 153–155; NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 10, Section 10.2, printed pp. 163–164.]

pictures.alt: A concave lens spreads real rays apart; their dashed backward extensions meet between F1 and O at a smaller, upright virtual image.
pictures.caption: A concave lens forms a smaller, erect virtual image between its focus and optical centre.

title: Image Formation by a Concave Lens

body:
New Cartesian Sign Convention for Lenses

Lenses use the New Cartesian Sign Convention, with distances measured from the optical centre O rather than from the pole of a mirror.

For the usual arrangement, light travels from left to right, and the real object is placed to the left of the lens.

  • Distances measured to the right of O are positive.
  • Distances measured to the left of O are negative.
  • Heights above the principal axis are positive.
  • Heights below the principal axis are negative.
  • For a real object on the left, object distance u is negative.
  • Convex lens focal length f is positive.
  • Concave lens focal length f is negative.

A real image formed on the right side of a lens has positive image distance v. A virtual image formed on the same side as the real object has negative v.

Lens Formula

The lens formula relates the focal length f, object distance u and image distance v of a thin spherical lens.

$$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}$$

It is valid for the usual thin-lens approximation when the signs are assigned according to the New Cartesian Sign Convention.

The mirror formula and lens formula are different. The mirror formula contains the sum \(1/v+1/u\), while the lens formula contains the difference \(1/v-1/u\).

Magnification of a Lens

The magnification of a lens is the ratio of signed image height h' to object height h.

$$m=\frac{h'}{h}=\frac{v}{u}$$

The sign of magnification describes the orientation of the image.

  • Positive m: Image is erect. For an ordinary real object, the image is virtual.
  • Negative m: Image is inverted and real.
  • Magnitude greater than 1: Image is enlarged.
  • Magnitude less than 1: Image is diminished.

For example, if \(u=-20\text{ cm}\) and \(v=+40\text{ cm}\), then:

$$m=\frac{+40}{-20}=-2$$

The image is real, inverted and twice the size of the object.

Power of a Lens

Power of a lens measures its ability to converge or diverge light rays. It is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length expressed in metres.

$$P=\frac{1}{f}$$

Here P represents lens power and f is the focal length in metres.

The SI unit of lens power is the dioptre (D).

$$1\text{ D}=1\text{ m}^{-1}$$

A lens of focal length 1 m has a power of 1 D in magnitude.

Positive and Negative Lens Power

A convex lens has positive focal length and therefore positive power. A concave lens has negative focal length and negative power.

One-step power calculations

A convex lens of focal length +0.50 m has power:

$$P=\frac{1}{+0.50}=+2\text{ D}$$

A concave lens of focal length -0.25 m has power:

$$P=\frac{1}{-0.25}=-4\text{ D}$$

The positive sign identifies the converging lens, while the negative sign identifies the diverging lens.

Relation Between Focal Length and Power

Power is inversely proportional to focal length. For lenses of the same type in the same surrounding medium, a smaller focal-length magnitude corresponds to a greater power magnitude.

Thus, a +4 D convex lens converges parallel light more strongly than a +2 D convex lens. A -4 D concave lens diverges light more strongly than a -2 D concave lens.

The sign describes whether the lens is converging or diverging. The magnitude describes how strongly it changes the direction of light.

Final Comparison: Mirrors and Lenses

FeatureMirrorLens
PrincipleReflectionRefraction
Reference pointPole POptical centre O
Formula\(1/f=1/v+1/u\)\(1/f=1/v-1/u\)
Magnification\(m=-v/u\)\(m=v/u\)
Converging typeConcave mirrorConvex lens
Diverging typeConvex mirrorConcave lens

Putting the Image-Formation Rules Together

For an ordinary real object, a plane mirror always produces a virtual, erect image of equal size. A convex mirror and a concave lens always produce virtual, erect and diminished images.

A concave mirror can produce a real, inverted image when the object is beyond its focus, or a virtual, erect and enlarged image when the object is inside its focus.

A convex lens behaves similarly in this respect: it produces a real, inverted image when the object is beyond its focal length, and a virtual, erect and enlarged image when the object is within its focal length.

These image rules, together with the laws of reflection and refraction, the sign conventions and the corresponding formulas, provide the basic framework for solving school-level objective questions on geometrical optics.

Prelims focus

  • Lens formula: \(1/f=1/v-1/u\).
  • Lens magnification: \(m=v/u\).
  • Power of a lens: \(P=1/f\), with f in metres.
  • Unit of power: dioptre; 1 D = 1 m-1.
  • Convex lens power is positive; concave lens power is negative.
  • Trap: Do not interchange the mirror and lens formulas or their magnification expressions.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.2.1–9.2.4 and 9.3.4–9.3.8, especially Equations 9.1–9.3 and 9.8–9.11, printed pp. 137–159; IIT Kanpur SATHEE, 'Light – Reflection and Refraction', Sections 9.3.6–9.3.8, consulted 2 November 2026.]
